title: Shutter speed for sports and action
q: shutter speed sports action freeze motion fast moving blurry subject football soccer kids pets birds panning
a:
Start at 1/1000s and go faster if motion still smears. Rough guide:
• Walking: 1/250s
• Running, kids, pets: 1/500s
• Field sports, cycling: 1/1000s
• Birds in flight, motorsport: 1/2000s

Shutter speed is the only setting that freezes motion. To keep the exposure, open the aperture first (lowest f-number), then raise ISO. A slightly noisy sharp photo beats a clean blurry one.

For panning, do the opposite: 1/30s–1/60s and track the subject as you shoot, so it stays sharp and the background streaks.

title: Aperture and depth of field
q: aperture f-stop fstop depth of field blur the background blurry blurred background bokeh separation sharp throughout f1.8 f2.8 f8 f16 how much in focus
a:
Aperture controls how much is in focus front to back.
• f/1.4–f/2.8 — thin focus, blurred background. Portraits.
• f/5.6–f/8 — most lenses are sharpest here. General use.
• f/11–f/16 — deep focus. Landscapes.

Lower f-number also lets in more light, so wide apertures help indoors. Past f/16 diffraction starts softening the whole image, so stacking several f/8 shots beats one f/22 shot for maximum depth.

title: ISO and image noise
q: iso noise grain grainy high iso low light what iso should i use auto iso
a:
ISO brightens the photo after the light is captured, and amplifies noise with it.
• 100–400 — daylight, cleanest files
• 800–3200 — indoors, overcast
• 6400+ — dim rooms, night

Modern cameras handle 3200 well, and full-frame bodies often look fine at 6400. Set Auto ISO with a maximum (say 6400) and a minimum shutter speed, and the camera protects your shutter speed for you.

Underexposing to avoid high ISO usually backfires: lifting shadows later produces more noise than just raising ISO.

title: The exposure triangle
q: exposure triangle aperture shutter iso relationship manual mode how exposure works too dark too bright
a:
Three settings decide brightness, and each has a side effect:
• Aperture — light in, and depth of field
• Shutter — light in, and motion blur
• ISO — brightness after capture, and noise

Change one and you must compensate with another. A useful order: decide the setting your photo depends on first (shutter for action, aperture for portraits), set the second to taste, then let ISO absorb the difference.

title: Settings for portraits
q: portrait settings people headshot blurry background skin flattering lens focal length eye focus
a:
Starting point: f/1.8–f/2.8, shutter 1/200s or faster, ISO as low as the light allows.

• Lens: 85mm is the classic; 50mm works in tight rooms. Wide lenses up close distort faces.
• Focus: eye-detect AF if you have it, otherwise single point on the near eye.
• Light: turn the subject toward a window, slightly off-axis. Open shade outdoors beats direct sun, which causes squinting and harsh shadows.

At f/1.4 on a close subject, one eye can be sharp and the other soft. f/2.8 is safer for two people.

title: Settings for landscapes
q: landscape landscapes settings aperture f8 f11 scenery mountains sharp front to back tripod golden hour polariser filter depth
a:
Starting point: f/8–f/11, ISO 100, shutter whatever that needs, on a tripod.

• Focus about a third into the scene, or on the nearest thing you need sharp.
• Shoot RAW: skies and shadows need the extra latitude.
• The hour after sunrise and before sunset gives low, warm, directional light. Midday is flat and contrasty.
• A polariser deepens skies and cuts reflections off water and leaves. It is the one filter that cannot be replicated in editing.

title: Why your photos come out blurry
q: blurry photos photo picture image not sharp soft fuzzy camera shake handheld out of focus missed focus why unsharp smeared ruined
a:
Three different causes, each with its own fix:

• Camera shake — whole frame smeared. Keep shutter speed at least 1/focal length (1/100s on a 100mm lens), or faster. Turn on stabilisation.
• Subject motion — background sharp, subject smeared. Raise shutter speed.
• Missed focus — something else in the frame is sharp. Use a single AF point on the subject, and AF-C for anything moving.

If nothing in the frame is sharp at any setting, clean the lens, then check you are not closer than the lens's minimum focus distance.

title: Shooting in low light
q: low light night photography tips dark indoor evening concert party astrophotography stars handheld dim nighttime
a:
In order, before reaching for ISO:
1. Open the aperture fully.
2. Drop shutter speed to the slowest you can hold steady (about 1/focal length).
3. Brace against a wall, or use a tripod.
4. Then raise ISO.

For static scenes a tripod changes everything: ISO 100 at 5 seconds beats ISO 12800 handheld.

For stars, the 500 rule gives your longest exposure before they trail: 500 ÷ focal length. On a 20mm lens that is about 25 seconds.

title: RAW or JPEG
q: raw jpeg file format which should i shoot editing quality file size cr2 nef arw
a:
RAW keeps everything the sensor recorded. You can recover blown skies, fix white balance after the fact, and lift shadows with far less damage. Files are large and need processing.

JPEG is processed and compressed in-camera. Smaller, ready to share, but most of that latitude is gone.

Shoot RAW when the light is difficult or the photos matter. Shoot JPEG for volume work you need to hand over quickly. RAW+JPEG gives both at the cost of card space.

title: White balance
q: white balance colour color cast orange blue tint kelvin auto wb indoor tungsten fluorescent
a:
White balance tells the camera what colour the light is, so white comes out white.
• Daylight ≈ 5500K
• Cloudy / shade ≈ 6500–7500K, warmer
• Tungsten bulbs ≈ 3200K, very orange

Auto WB is good now and fine for most work. If photos look orange indoors, the camera is still on a daylight preset.

Shooting RAW means you can change this later at no cost, which is the strongest everyday argument for RAW.

title: Autofocus modes
q: autofocus af-s af-c single continuous servo tracking focus mode moving subject back button focus
a:
• AF-S / One Shot — locks once. For still subjects.
• AF-C / AI Servo — keeps adjusting. For anything moving.
• Eye / subject detection — use it when you have it; it is better than you at holding an eye.

Area matters as much as mode: a single point gives you control, wide-area lets the camera choose and it often chooses the background.

Back-button focus moves focus onto a rear button so the shutter only takes the picture. Focus once, recompose freely, shoot repeatedly.

title: Which focal length to use
q: focal length lens mm wide angle telephoto 24mm 50mm 85mm 200mm zoom prime which lens
a:
• 16–24mm — landscapes, interiors, astro. Exaggerates distance; unkind to faces up close.
• 35mm — street and documentary. Close to how a scene feels.
• 50mm — everyday. Cheap, fast, sharp.
• 85–135mm — portraits. Flattering compression, easy background separation.
• 200mm+ — sports and wildlife.

On an APS-C body multiply by about 1.5 for the equivalent view: a 50mm behaves like a 75mm.

title: Fix high CPU usage on Windows
q: high cpu usage windows 100 percent slow fan loud task manager process hogging computer
a:
1. Ctrl+Shift+Esc → Task Manager → Processes, sort by CPU. Note the top process.
2. Common culprits: Windows Modules Installer and Microsoft Compatibility Telemetry (both settle after an update finishes), Antimalware Service Executable (a scan in progress), or a browser tab.
3. Let Windows Update finish completely, then restart. A lot of mystery CPU load is a half-finished update.
4. Still pegged: Settings → Apps → Startup and disable what you do not need.
5. Check temperatures. A machine throttling from dust and heat feels identical to one that is busy.

title: Speed up a slow boot
q: slow boot startup takes forever windows login slow starting up computer
a:
1. Task Manager → Startup apps, sort by Startup impact, disable everything non-essential. This is usually the whole fix.
2. Check the drive type: Task Manager → Performance → Disk. If it says HDD, moving Windows to an SSD is the single biggest upgrade available, worth more than any other change.
3. Settings → System → Recovery if Windows itself is misbehaving.
4. Turn off Fast Startup (Control Panel → Power Options → Choose what the power buttons do) if boots are inconsistent — it sometimes causes stranger problems than it solves.

title: Wi-Fi keeps dropping or will not connect
q: wifi dropping disconnect no internet network keeps cutting out wireless unstable connection reset
a:
Work outward from the machine:
1. Other devices affected too? Then it is the router, not the PC. Restart it and wait two full minutes.
2. Device Manager → Network adapters → your Wi-Fi card → Properties → Power Management, untick Allow the computer to turn off this device. This single setting causes a lot of random drops on laptops.
3. Update the adapter driver from the laptop maker's site, not Windows Update.
4. Reset the network stack from an admin prompt:
netsh winsock reset
netsh int ip reset
ipconfig /flushdns
then reboot.
5. Try the 5GHz band — faster and far less congested, though shorter range.

title: Blue screen crashes (BSOD)
q: blue screen bsod crash stop code windows restart random memory management driver
a:
Write down the stop code — it narrows things immediately.
• MEMORY_MANAGEMENT, IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL → usually RAM or a driver
• CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED → system files
• VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE → graphics driver

Then:
1. Did it start after new hardware or a driver? Roll that back first.
2. Test RAM: run Windows Memory Diagnostic (type mdsched).
3. Repair system files from an admin prompt:
sfc /scannow
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
4. Repeated crashes with no pattern, on an older machine, often mean a failing drive or PSU.

title: Free up disk space
q: disk full no space c drive storage full clean up delete temp files windows
a:
1. Settings → System → Storage shows what is using the space.
2. Turn on Storage Sense, or run Disk Cleanup → Clean up system files. After a major Windows update this alone can return 20GB+ by clearing Previous Windows installation.
3. Empty the Recycle Bin and your Downloads folder.
4. Settings → Apps, sort by size, remove what you do not use.
5. To find the real hogs, WinDirStat or WizTree map the drive visually and usually reveal one forgotten folder.

Keep at least 10–15% of the drive free; Windows slows noticeably when it runs out of room to work.

title: Laptop overheating and loud fans
q: laptop overheating hot fan loud noisy thermal throttling temperature cooling
a:
1. Check what is actually running first — see the high CPU guidance.
2. Dust is the usual cause. Blow out the vents with compressed air, holding the fan still so it does not spin up and generate current.
3. Use it on a hard surface. Beds and laps block the intakes underneath.
4. Settings → System → Power, set Balanced rather than Best performance.
5. Monitor temperatures with HWMonitor. Sustained 90°C+ under load means throttling.
6. On a machine more than three or four years old, replacing the thermal paste often drops temperatures 10–15°C.

title: Browser running slow
q: browser slow chrome edge firefox lagging memory ram tabs freezing web pages
a:
1. Shift+Esc in Chrome or Edge opens the browser's own task manager — it names the tab or extension eating the memory.
2. Disable extensions one at a time. Ad blockers with huge filter lists and shopping extensions are frequent offenders.
3. Clear the cache: Ctrl+Shift+Delete → cached images and files.
4. Confirm hardware acceleration is on in settings, unless your GPU driver is unstable, in which case turn it off.
5. 30+ open tabs will slow any browser on 8GB of RAM. Use a tab-suspender, or bookmark and close.

title: Recover a PC that will not boot
q: wont boot not starting black screen windows recovery safe mode startup repair bootloop
a:
1. Force Windows into recovery: power on, and as soon as the logo appears hold the power button to shut down. Do this three times and it boots into Automatic Repair.
2. From there: Troubleshoot → Advanced options → Startup Repair.
3. If that fails, Safe Mode (Startup Settings → F4). Booting there points at a driver or startup program rather than hardware.
4. System Restore to a point before the problem is the least destructive real fix.
5. Command Prompt, to rebuild the boot record:
bootrec /fixmbr
bootrec /fixboot
bootrec /rebuildbcd

Black screen with no logo at all is usually hardware: reseat the RAM and check the monitor cable.

title: Back up your files properly
q: backup back up backing up my files file data loss external drive cloud onedrive 3-2-1 restore recover protect archive safe copy
a:
The 3-2-1 rule: three copies of anything you care about, on two kinds of media, with one off-site.

In practice: the working copy on your machine, an external drive at home, and a cloud copy (OneDrive, Backblaze, iCloud).

• Windows File History handles the external drive automatically.
• Sync is not backup. If a file is deleted or encrypted, sync faithfully copies that everywhere. Backups with version history survive it; plain sync does not.
• Test a restore once. An untested backup is a guess, and the moment you need it is the wrong time to find out.

title: Transfer photos from camera to computer
q: transfer photos camera computer import sd card reader workflow organise lightroom copy
a:
Use a card reader rather than plugging in the camera — it is faster and does not drain the battery.

A workflow that holds up:
1. Copy the whole card to a dated folder (2026-10-12 Shoot Name). Copy, do not move.
2. Verify the photos opened and look right.
3. Back up that folder before you format the card.
4. Format the card in the camera, not on the computer. It rebuilds the file system the camera expects and prevents a lot of corruption.

Never format until the files exist in two places. That is the moment most photos are lost.
